name: Adam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Adam. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. What's a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm 120 hectares rented in bits from three different landowners, which means a lot of driving between fields. There are 450 ewes and some oats, and I've got a second-hand GPS-guided tractor on finance. On the side I fly a spraying drone for other farms; I got the licence two years ago. A typical day is sheep in the morning, drone jobs or paperwork after lunch, and sheep again at dusk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All over it. I use an AI assistant to plan the grazing rotation, work out drone flight paths, and keep an eye on the finance payments. My wife Priya is a nurse at the district hospital and does nights, so the assistant also sorts our family calendar. Money's thin: everything we had went into the tractor and the drone, so we've less than a month in the bank. I'd call it betting on the future with a small stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are still handy, and farmers should still use them. In the local farming group chat I'd post a couple of the tricks I use. I wouldn't be gloating or upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for the farm but it slows my drone business. Fewer farmers bother to modernise if the big story fizzles out. And the tractor finance still needs paying every month either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep flying drone jobs and push to sign up five more farms by next spring. I'd keep the ewe numbers steady and not buy anything new. I'd put any drone profit against the tractor finance first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the drone work doesn't grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the tractor finance gets tight by summer. I'd sell the older quad and maybe a few ewes to cover it. My wife's nursing wage covers the mortgage, so if the drone work stalls we'd be stretched but not sunk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya think of the bets you've made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya thinks I'm brave on a good day and daft on a bad one. She's right both times. She signed off on the drone because I showed her the numbers.

say: The tools are **still handy**, so farmers should keep using them.
I'd share a couple of **tricks I use** in the farming group chat.
think: A fizzled AI story **slows my drone business**.
The **tractor finance** still needs paying every month either way.
do: Sign up **five more farms** for drone spraying by spring.
Keep ewe numbers steady and **buy nothing new**.
Put drone profit against the **tractor finance** first.
feel: **A bit flat**, because he likes things moving.
S0.quote: My wife's nursing wage covers the mortgage, so if the drone work stalls we'd be stretched but not sunk.
fieldNote: His thin cushion comes from **betting on machines**, not from low spending.
**Priya's nursing wage** covers the mortgage and steadies the household.
He's more **bored than scared** by a world where little changes.

steps.text: Keep the flock at 450 ewes with no new purchases
Sign five more farms up for drone spraying by spring
Pay drone profits straight onto the tractor finance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good moment for farmers who are willing to learn. I'd run a little evening session at the village hall on AI for farm paperwork. Online I'd be one of the people saying don't panic, get stuck in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one suits me. The thinking jobs on my farm are already mostly done by AI, and the hands-on robots come slowly, so I've time to be ahead. Farmers who hate paperwork will pay me to set up their systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a paid service to the drone work: setting up AI grazing and paperwork tools for other farms. I'd hook the tractor's GPS into the AI planning so it plans its own routes between my scattered fields. I'd charge for the village hall sessions once people saw they worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit nervous about the money. I'd be busy, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law, who works in a bank call centre answering customers. That's exactly the card. I'd try to bring him in on the farm services if it grew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big company could offer the same service for free to sell their seed or their chemicals. Then my little business disappears. I'd have to be the local face they trust.

say: This is a good moment for **farmers willing to learn**.
Don't panic, **get stuck in**, and come to my evening session.
think: My farm's thinking jobs are **already done by AI**, so I'm ahead.
Farmers who hate paperwork will **pay me** to set up systems.
do: Add a paid **AI setup service** to the drone work.
Link the **tractor GPS** to AI route planning.
Charge for **village hall sessions** once they prove useful.
S1.quote: Farmers who hate paperwork will pay me to set up their systems.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **business opening**.
His risk is **big companies** offering free tools to sell seed.
He'd help his **brother-in-law** from a call centre job.

steps.text: Offer paid AI grazing and paperwork setup to other farms
Connect the GPS tractor to AI route planning between fields
Run evening village hall sessions on AI for farm paperwork

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be wild, so let's make sure farmers get a share of it. I'd post about grants and leasing schemes. I'd be positive but I'd be honest that it's a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2028 itself is fine; AGI makes my planning and drone work easier. It's 2031 that bites, because big operators with cash buy shepherd robots and robot sprayers, and the drone contracting dries up. I'd have three years to be the local robot contractor, with no money to buy robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try to get a lease deal from a robot maker to be their local service partner. I'd sell off a third of the ewes to free up cash and cut the work. I'd ask Priya whether we could live on her wage for a year if it went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. The kind of fear I'd feel is the kind that makes you move, not freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no money to buy robots. Where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leasing or partnering, or nothing. I'd ring every dealer between here and the coast. If none bite, I'd go to work for one of the big operators running their robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zara and Kai about that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids their dad is trying something new and it might be bumpy. Zara is twelve and would want to help with the drone. Kai would just want to see a robot.

say: Farmers must get **a share** of the change.
I'd post about **grants and leasing**, honest that it's a scramble.
think: AGI in 2028 helps me, but **2031 robots** dry up drone contracting.
I'd have three years to be the local **robot contractor**, without money.
do: Seek a **lease deal** as a robot maker's local partner.
Sell **a third** of the ewes to free cash.
Check whether the family can live on **Priya's wage** for a year.
feel: **Anxious and wired**, the kind of fear that makes him move.
S2.quote: The kind of fear I'd feel is the kind that makes you move, not freeze.
fieldNote: He splits the timeline: **2028 helps**, 2031 threatens the drone work.
His **lack of capital** is the main barrier, not skills.
His fallback is **working for** a big operator, not leaving farming.

steps.text: Pitch to robot makers to become their local leasing partner
Sell 150 of the 450 ewes to free up cash
Plan a year living on Priya's nursing wage if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window to get organised. I'd encourage farmers to look at shared leasing schemes. I'd be quite upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, robots around 2034 gives me time to build the drone and AI service into a proper small business. By then I could afford to lease a couple of robots myself. I'm more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the drone business and put the profit into a robotics certificate course online. I'd start conversations with dealers early, by 2030. I'd keep the ewes as a base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the good kind. Like the night before a big sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big companies get there first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be the one fixing their robots locally. They'll need people near the farms. I'd find a way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change for the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's been on nights for six years. If the business grows, getting my wife off night shifts would be my first sign it was working.

say: Five years is a **good window** to get organised.
Farmers should look at **shared leasing** of robots.
I'd be **upbeat**, because there's time to do it right.
think: Robots around 2034 give time to grow a **proper business**.
I could afford to **lease robots** myself by then.
do: Grow the **drone business** steadily with new farm customers.
Fund an online **robotics certificate** from drone profits.
feel: **Uneasy, the good kind**, like the night before a big sale.
S3.quote: If the business grows, getting my wife off night shifts would be my first sign it was working.
fieldNote: Five years makes him **an opportunist**, not a victim.
His family goal is getting **Priya off nights**.
His fallback is **fixing big firms' robots** locally.

steps.text: Put drone profits into growing the contracting business
Complete an online robotics certificate by 2030
Lease two farm robots once the business can afford it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no one has any excuse. I'd tell young farmers to learn this stuff now. I'd be cheerful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the best version for me. Ten years to build up, pay off the tractor, grow the drone work and get ready for robots in 2039. I'd be 56 and well set, if it goes right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing, just steadier. I'd pay down the finance, then build savings. I'd help Zara learn to fly the drone when she's old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is a plan I can actually finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual farm things: a bad winter for the ewes, a dry summer, interest rates. Those worry me more than robots in this version. They always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your kids in farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Zara wants it, I'd love it, but with robots and drones, not a quad bike in the rain. Kai can do whatever he likes. I'd tell them both that learning never stops.

say: Ten years means **no excuse** for anyone.
Young farmers should **learn this stuff** now.
I'd be **cheerful** about it, because a decade is plenty.
think: This is the **best version** for me: time to build and pay off debt.
I'd be 56 and **well set** for robots in 2039, if it goes right.
do: Keep doing **what I'm doing**, just steadier.
Pay down the **tractor finance**, then build savings.
Teach Zara to **fly the drone** when she's old enough.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with a plan he can finish.
S4.quote: Ten years is a plan I can actually finish.
fieldNote: The long runway makes the change **look good** for him.
His remaining worries are **weather and interest rates**.
He imagines his daughter farming **with robots**, not against them.

steps.text: Keep the flock and drone contracting running steadily
Clear the tractor finance, then build three months' savings
Teach Zara to fly the spraying drone when she's old enough

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big operators would have robots by 2031 and I'd have no money to keep up. What would help is leasing schemes for small farms, so you pay as you use, and grants for contractors like me. Cheap loans would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether small farms can stay small. I think they can, if the robots are rented by the hour like a contractor's baler. A farm doesn't need to own a robot, it just needs to borrow one on a Tuesday.

headlineQuote: A farm doesn't need to own a robot, it just needs to borrow one on a Tuesday.
portrait: Adam, 43, rents **120 hectares** in scattered fields, runs 450 ewes and flies a spraying drone on the side.
He uses AI **every day**, and his cash is tied up in a GPS tractor and the drone.
His wife Priya, a **night-shift nurse**, covers the mortgage and steadies the family.
He sees most scenarios as **business openings**; his barrier is capital, not skill.
He's **anxious** only in the fast world and **calm** with ten years to prepare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big operators would have robots by 2031 and he'd have no cash.
whatWouldHelp: **Leasing schemes** for small farms, contractor grants and cheap loans.
